patch.value: Every pm next and pm context read writes one usage-ledger row per open item under a single global lock, and the compaction trigger is a byte threshold that a count-based retention can never satisfy

The context usage ledger at .agents/pm/runtime/context-usage.jsonl is the substrate the usage-affinity signal reads, and it is written on the read path. Measured at HEAD. One pm next serve entry is 10,377 bytes and carries 200 candidate rows. One pm context serve entry is 16,298 bytes and carries 315 rows, which is exactly the open item count, so the per-read write is O(open items) with no cap on the context surface while next caps at 200. The retention policy in src/sdk/context-usage.ts keeps the last 2,048 events, but compaction is triggered by DEFAULT_COMPACTION_BYTES of 262,144 bytes. The live ledger is 1,224,242 bytes, 4.7 times its own trigger, so the trigger fires on essentially every read and the count-based retention can never bring the file back under it. Each firing acquires the global context-usage-ledger lock, appends, then reads and parses the entire file, filters it, serializes it to a temporary file and renames. At steady state with modern entry sizes the retained set is about 2,048 times 13 kB, roughly 27 MB, so the mature behaviour is a full read-parse-rewrite of a 27 MB file inside a global lock on every context or next call. Extrapolated to the stated target of a million open items, one context read writes a single entry of roughly 50 MB and the ring retains 2,048 of them. Measured contention today: twelve concurrent pm next calls complete in 5,145 ms against a 1,013 ms serial single call, and no entries were lost or corrupted, so this is a throughput ceiling rather than a correctness failure. The write is correctly wrapped in a try block at next.ts:507 and context.ts:2582 so a lock timeout degrades the signal instead of failing the read. This is the cost and scaling of the ledger. It is not the propensity signal correctness, and it is not fleet-amortized assembly, which is pm-tch9cs.

A serve entry records a bounded number of candidate rows independent of open item count, and the bound is declared in the contract rather than implied by a surface; Retention and compaction are expressed in the same unit, so the trigger threshold is reachable by the policy that follows it and the ledger has a declared steady-state ceiling in bytes; The read path does not rewrite the whole ledger on every serve, proved by measuring bytes written per read at three corpus sizes including the million-item tier; Ledger writes are measured under a concurrent fleet at the scale target and the published numbers state reads per second per workspace and the observed lock wait distribution; A negative control proves the declared ceiling gate fails when a surface reintroduces one row per open item
